The back room of Kenealy's café smelled of copper tubing, burnt sugar, and something older than either — something that had no proper name in the English language, though Riley claimed it had one in a dialect of Gaelic that hadn't been spoken aloud since the reign of a king nobody remembered.

Con Lantry knew better than to go back there.

He went back there anyway.

It had been a Tuesday of the particular cruelty that only Tuesdays in November can manage. The rain came sideways. The gas lamps on Mulberry Street threw orange smears across the wet cobblestones, and the few souls who pushed through Kenealy's front door arrived looking like they'd been wrung out by an indifferent hand. Con served them their whiskies and their stouts and their hot toddies with the quiet, meticulous grace that had made him, at twenty-six, the most reliable bartender in the neighbourhood and, by nearly universal agreement, the most invisible.

He was not unhandsome. That was the tragedy of it, or at least one of the tragedies. Con Lantry had good bones, as his mother had told him, and dark eyes that caught the light in an interesting way, and hands that were steady and sure on the glass. But he carried himself like a man perpetually expecting to be asked to leave a room he had no business being in, shoulders slightly rounded, gaze aimed at the middle distance, voice calibrated to a register that required customers to lean forward slightly to hear him, which he secretly preferred because it meant they were closer to the bar and less likely to linger.

Katherine Doyle had been coming to Kenealy's for three months.

She worked at the milliner's two doors down, and she came in on Tuesdays and Thursdays for a glass of warm cider after closing, and she always sat at the far end of the bar where the light was best, and she always brought a book, and she always said *thank you, Con* when he set her glass down, using his name with a casual familiarity that made his chest do something structurally unsound.

He had composed, in the privacy of his own skull, approximately forty-seven conversations with Katherine Doyle. They ranged from the practical — *I notice you're reading Dickens, I've always thought Dickens was* — to the frankly delusional — *Katherine, I have been meaning to tell you for some time now that you are the most* — and not one of them had ever made it past his teeth. Instead he said things like *there you are* and *another cider, then* and *mind the step on your way out, it's slippery in the rain*, and Katherine smiled at him in a way that suggested she found him pleasant and harmless, which was, he had decided, the worst possible thing a woman could find a man.

Tonight she was reading something with a red cover, and she had her chin resting in her hand, and there was a small ink stain on her left index finger, and Con Lantry had been staring at that ink stain for twenty minutes while mechanically polishing the same glass.

Riley and McQuirk had been in the back room since Thursday.

This was not unusual. Riley and McQuirk were in the back room with some regularity, by arrangement with old Kenealy himself, who was either a man of extraordinary open-mindedness or one who had simply stopped asking questions that made his head hurt. They were alchemists, or they called themselves alchemists, or perhaps the word was *distillers* of an unusually philosophical bent. They had equipment back there that clinked and hissed at odd hours, and they occasionally emerged to use the facilities or to ask Con for his professional opinion on something they'd decanted into a small glass, and Con always gave his honest opinion, which they always ignored.

But tonight something was different.

Con could smell it from the bar. Not the usual sharp medicinal bite of their experiments, not the sulphurous near-disasters that had twice required the opening of all the windows. This was something else entirely. It was warm and golden in character — he could smell *colour*, which he understood was not scientifically possible, and yet — it smelled of autumn afternoons and the last good day before winter sets in permanently, and something underneath that he couldn't name, something that felt like the precise moment before you say the thing you've been meaning to say.
